title: CBC Red Cell Indices, WBC Differential, Platelets, and Analyzer Histograms
summary: How the complete blood count is built: red cell indices and their formulas, the automated and manual white cell differential, platelet counting pitfalls such as EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia, and how histograms and instrument flags guide smear review.
objectives: Calculate and interpret RBC indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW) from red cell count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit.
Describe the normal WBC differential and the morphologic clues that trigger manual review.
Explain common platelet counting artifacts and how to resolve them.
Use histograms and analyzer flags to decide when a peripheral smear review is required.

highYield: MCV (fL) = hematocrit / RBC count; MCH (pg) = hemoglobin / RBC count; MCHC (g/dL) = hemoglobin / hematocrit — indices classify anemia as microcytic, normocytic, or macrocytic.
RDW reflects red cell size distribution; an elevated RDW suggests mixed or developing populations (e.g., iron deficiency) rather than a uniform trait.
EDTA-dependent platelet clumping causes pseudothrombocytopenia; a smear shows clumps and a citrate tube usually resolves the count.
Analyzer flags (atypical lymphocytes, blasts, nucleated RBCs, platelet clumps, microcytic interference) are prompts for smear review, not diagnoses.
Reference intervals for all CBC parameters vary by age, sex, altitude, population, and analyzer; verify against your local laboratory.

quickReview.mnemonic: Indices: MCV = size, MCH/MCHC = color, RDW = variety.

deepStudy.introduction: The CBC is the most ordered test in the laboratory, and its power comes from derived relationships. The analyzer counts cells and measures hemoglobin, then computes indices that classify red cells by size and hemoglobin content; it produces a differential and a platelet count, and it displays histograms that act as quality control eyes on every specimen. The art of hematology is knowing when to trust the number, when to check the smear, and when to redraw the patient.

sections.heading: Red cell indices and what they mean
sections.body: The analyzer measures red cell count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit (packed cell volume) and derives three classical indices. MCV describes mean cell volume: values below the local lower limit define microcytosis (classically below about 80 fL in adults), values above the upper limit macrocytosis (classically above about 100 fL), with method-specific reference intervals. MCH describes mean hemoglobin content per cell and MCHC the mean hemoglobin concentration per volume of packed red cells; MCHC is the most physiologically stable index, and markedly elevated values suggest spherocytosis, cold agglutinin interference, or specimen problems. RDW quantifies anisocytosis: in iron deficiency, RDW typically rises early, while in thalassemia trait the cells are microcytic but remarkably uniform (normal RDW), a classic discriminator. Calculated hematocrit (RBC count multiplied by MCV) generally agrees with measured hematocrit; discrepancies suggest analyzer issues or abnormal plasma volume. Indices must always be read with the local reference interval, which varies with age, sex, pregnancy, altitude, and smoking status.

sections.heading: The white cell differential
sections.body: The automated differential classifies leukocytes by size, conductivity, and light scatter (or by fluorescent staining in newer platforms), reporting neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils as percentages and absolute counts. Absolute counts are clinically more useful than percentages: a normal percentage with a high white cell count can still represent neutrophilia. Morphologic flags appear when the population falls outside expected patterns: atypical lymphocytes (reactive lymphocytes in viral infections), blasts (immature cells demanding smear review and possible flow cytometry), left shift with band forms (immature neutrophils suggesting infection or marrow stress), and toxic changes (toxic granulation, Dohle bodies, cytoplasmic vacuolization in severe infection). Hypersegmented neutrophils suggest megaloblastic process. Nucleated red cells are counted separately and require correction of the white cell count. The manual differential on a stained smear remains the reference for confirmation, and a 100-cell differential reports percentages with imprecision that must be understood at low counts. Automated differentials are efficient but cannot replace morphology when flags or clinical suspicion suggest abnormal cells.

sections.heading: Platelets and counting artifacts
sections.body: Platelets are counted by impedance or optical methods and reported with mean platelet volume. Common artifacts must be recognized: EDTA-induced platelet clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia) produces a spuriously low count and an analyzer flag; the smear shows platelet clumps, and recollection into a citrate or heparin tube, or blood drawn in a different anticoagulant, resolves it. Giant platelets (as in immune thrombocytopenia or myelodysplasia) may be counted as red cells by impedance, underestimating the count; optical or fluorescent methods and smear estimates help. Marked leukocytosis or microcytosis can interfere with platelet histograms. Platelet satellitism (platelets adhering to neutrophils in EDTA) is another rare cause of spuriously low counts. Conversely, thrombocytosis is reactive (inflammation, iron deficiency, splenectomy, malignancy) or clonal (essential thrombocythemia), and morphology (size, clustering) and clinical context differentiate them. Platelet counts are also subject to reference interval variation by age and population, and critical values follow local policy. When the analyzer count and the smear disagree, estimate platelets on the smear and document the discrepancy so the clinician receives a trustworthy number.

sections.heading: Histograms, flags, and when to review the smear
sections.body: Automated analyzers generate frequency-distribution histograms for red cells, white cells, and platelets. The red cell histogram shows a single population in health; a dimorphic shoulder suggests two red cell populations (recent transfusion, mixed deficiency, sideroblastic process). The white cell histogram separates lymphocyte, mononuclear, and granulocyte regions; flags arise when events fall in indeterminate zones, as with atypical lymphocytes, blasts, or nucleated red cells. The platelet histogram can be truncated by microcytes, fragments, or giant platelets. Flags are not diagnoses: their purpose is to route specimens to smear review. Instrument performance also varies by counting principle: impedance counts by volume, optical methods by light scatter and fluorescence (better for abnormal cells), and each has documented limitations in extreme counts and abnormal populations. Reticulocyte counts (RNA-based fluorescence) and the reticulocyte production index help assess marrow response in anemia, correcting for the degree of anemia and maturation time. Every laboratory defines its own flag criteria and smear-review rules in its procedure manual; these rules are part of quality assurance.

deepStudy.clinicalSignificance: Index patterns diagnose anemias at a glance (microcytic hypochromic vs macrocytic), platelet artifacts prevent unnecessary treatment (you do not transfuse a clumped-tube pseudothrombocytopenia), and smear review catches blasts that change a patient's life in minutes. Correcting the white cell count for nucleated red cells prevents dangerous underestimation of leukocytosis in neonates and marrow-stress states.
deepStudy.labInterpretation: Report indices with units and local reference intervals; flag critical results per policy. Correlate automated results with smear morphology whenever flags appear, and document clumping or hemolysis. Interpret absolute neutrophil counts rather than percentages when assessing infection risk. Reference intervals vary by laboratory, analyzer, age, sex, altitude, and population — always verify locally.

examTraps: A low platelet count in EDTA blood is not automatically thrombocytopenia: check the smear for clumps and recollect in citrate before acting.
Correct the white cell count for nucleated red cells (the analyzer may count nRBCs as WBCs) before interpreting leukocytosis.
MCV cutoffs for micro/macrocytosis are adult teaching values; pediatric and neonatal intervals differ by age.

memoryHooks.text: MCV = size (small vs big), MCH/MCHC = color (pale vs red), RDW = variety (uniform vs mixed).
memoryHooks.funny: MCV ang size, MCH ang kulay, RDW ang variety show. Parang damit sa ukay: may maliit, may maputla, may halo-halo.

memoryHooks.text: EDTA clumps platelets like students during a surprise quiz — count them in citrate instead and the truth appears.
memoryHooks.funny: Platelet clumping: nag-tago ang platelets sa tuhod ng neutrophils. Citrate tube = bagong classroom, doon sila magbibilang ng maayos. Wag mag-panic agad, smear muna.
